plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 1.1.7
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels, (a), (b), and (c), illustrating the approximation of the area under a curve by inscribed rectangles. Panel (a): a smooth curve over the interval [a, b] with the entire region between the curve and the x-axis shaded. Panel (b): the same curve with a small number of wide rectangles inscribed under it, giving a coarse Riemann sum approximation. Panel (c): the same curve with many narrow rectangles filling most of the gap, giving a much closer approximation to the true area. The figure introduces the Riemann sum approach to defining the definite integral as the limit of rectangular area approximations as the number of rectangles increases without bound.

demo_steps.title: The exact area
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a): the whole region between the curve and the x-axis from a to b is shaded. This is the quantity we want, but we have no formula for a region with a curved top.

demo_steps.title: A coarse approximation
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b): five inscribed rectangles whose areas we can compute exactly. Their total is close to the true area, but white slivers between each rectangle top and the curve show how much we are missing.

demo_steps.title: Many thin rectangles
demo_steps.narration: Panel (c): with about twenty-five narrower rectangles the staircase follows the curve closely and the leftover slivers are barely visible. The sum has moved noticeably nearer the exact area.

demo_steps.title: One panel, one motion
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the single animated panel and drag n yourself. Watch the Riemann sum readout climb toward the exact area while the error readout shrinks toward zero.

demo_steps.title: Sample point stops mattering
demo_steps.narration: At small n, left, midpoint, and right sampling give visibly different sums. Raise n and all three readouts collapse onto the same number — the limit is independent of the sampling rule.

demo_steps.title: The limit
demo_steps.narration: Play the refinement animation: the rectangles thin out until the staircase is indistinguishable from the shaded region. That limiting value is the definite integral of f from a to b.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The definite integral is not a new kind of area formula — it is the single number that rectangle sums are forced toward as the rectangles are made arbitrarily thin.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Clean white background, textbook style. In three-panel mode, place three identical axis systems side by side with captions (a), (b), (c) centered below each; in single-panel mode, one large centered axis system. Axes are thin black lines with arrowheads, y-axis labeled 'y' at top, x-axis labeled 'x' at right. The curve is a thick medium-blue (approx #29ABE2) smooth cubic-like shape: it enters low on the left, rises to a rounded maximum roughly one-third across, descends to a shallow minimum about three-quarters across, then rises again at the right edge; it extends slightly past both a and b. Interval endpoints a (left, just right of the y-axis) and b (right) are marked by italic serif labels below the x-axis with thin vertical segments up to the curve. Panel (a) shows the full region under the curve filled with pale blue (#CCE5F0). Panels (b) and (c) show inscribed rectangles with the same pale blue fill and thin black outlines, sitting on the x-axis, tops touching or falling just under the curve — (b) roughly five wide bars, (c) roughly twenty-five narrow bars. Uncovered slivers between bar tops and the curve stay white so the approximation error reads visually. In the single-panel interactive mode, overlay the faint exact shaded region behind the rectangles so the shrinking gap is obvious, and show a compact readout block (n, Riemann sum, exact area, error) in an upper corner. Highlight the error region in a light warm tint when it is large so the learner's eye is drawn to what the rectangles miss.

authoredPrompt: This figure contains three panels, (a), (b), and (c), illustrating the approximation of the area under a curve by inscribed rectangles. Panel (a): a smooth curve over the interval [a, b] with the entire region between the curve and the x-axis shaded. Panel (b): the same curve with a small number of wide rectangles inscribed under it, giving a coarse Riemann sum approximation. Panel (c): the same curve with many narrow rectangles filling most of the gap, giving a much closer approximation to the true area. The figure introduces the Riemann sum approach to defining the definite integral as the limit of rectangular area approximations as the number of rectangles increases without bound.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for number of rectangles n: watch the bars refine from coarse (panel b) to fine (panel c) and display the running Riemann sum value
- Toggle the three panels into a single animated view to eliminate side-by-side comparison
authoredContext: However, for regions with curved boundaries, such as that in Figure 1.1.7a, a more general approach is needed. One such approach is to begin by approximating the area of the region by inscribing a number of rectangles of equal width under the curve and adding the areas of these rectangles (Figure 1.1.7b). Intuition suggests that if we repeat that approximation process using more and more rectangles, then the rectangles will tend to fill in the gaps under the curve, and the approximations will get closer and closer to the exact area under the curve (Figure 1.1.7c). This suggests that we can define the area under the curve to be the limiting value of these approximations. This idea will be considered in detail later, but the point to note here is that once again the concept of a limit comes into play.

discrepancies: Panel aspect ratio is badly distorted: each of the three panels is far taller than wide, so the gentle broad hump-and-dip of the source curve renders as a steep V/W shape. At a glance the curve reads as a different function than the source's smooth sinusoidal wave.

Large empty vertical gap between the drawn axes (~y=400) and the (a)/(b)/(c) captions (~y=519); in the source the captions sit just below each panel, so the composition looks unbalanced and wastes half the canvas height.

Panel (b) draws 5 rectangles at the default step while the source shows 6 subintervals; also the source's rectangles are drawn with tops that cross the curve (left/endpoint-like sampling), whereas the default here is strictly inscribed, so the characteristic over/under-shoot of panel (b) is lost.

Rectangle outlines in panel (c) are drawn heavy enough relative to the very narrow panel that the thin-rectangle staircase reads as a solid hatched block rather than the light outlined slivers of the source.
The curve's minimum drops much closer to the x-axis than in the source, making the shaded region look like two lobes rather than one broad region with a shallow dip.
evaluation.notes: All three panels, the blue curve, light-blue fills, axes with arrowheads and a/b/x/y labels are correctly reproduced with excellent, pedagogically apt interactions (n slider, sampling rule, single-panel mode, refinement animation, 6-step demo), but the panels are rendered far too narrow and tall so the gentle source wave becomes a steep V and a large dead gap separates the artwork from the (a)/(b)/(c) captions.
action_items: Constrain each panel to a landscape aspect (roughly 3:2 width:height) — letterbox the drawing area vertically or reduce the canvas height — so the curve reproduces the source's broad hump and shallow dip instead of a steep V.
Move the (a)/(b)/(c) captions to sit directly beneath each panel's x-axis (reduce insB / caption offset) to eliminate the large empty band below the axes.

Default panel (b) to 6 subintervals and consider a non-inscribed default (left-endpoint or the source's crossing tops) so panel (b) matches the source's rectangle count and over/under-shoot appearance.
Scale rectangle stroke width down with panel width in panel (c) so the fine staircase reads as light outlines rather than a dense hatched mass.
plan_action_items: Specify a target drawing aspect ratio for the three-panel strip (wide and short, as in the source) rather than letting panels inherit the full container height.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual decomposition and interactions are correct; the issues are concrete rendering fixes (panel aspect ratio, caption placement, default subinterval count, stroke scaling) that belong to the generator.

discrepancies: The three panels render very small inside the available canvas (roughly 170 px wide each in a ~600 px area, with large empty margins above and below), so the whole figure reads as a thumbnail rather than a drop-in replacement for the full-width source figure.

As a consequence of the scaling, the italic axis labels x, y, a, b and the panel captions (a)/(b)/(c) are clamped near their minimum font size and are only marginally legible, whereas in the source they are large, prominent serif italics.

Panel (b) in the source shows a mix of over- and under-shooting rectangle tops (heights not all from one endpoint rule, with visible white gaps above some rectangles); the default left-endpoint rendering makes the staircase read slightly differently, though the composition is close.

The source curve descends visibly below the start of the shaded region at the far left (a short tail below y(a)) and rises steeply at the far right; the generated cosine is somewhat flatter/more symmetric, giving slightly different panel silhouettes.
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful three-panel Riemann-sum figure with excellent, pedagogically sound interactivity (n slider, sampling-rule select, single-panel toggle, stepped narration, refinement animation), but the drawing is scaled down into a small portion of the canvas so axis/endpoint labels and captions are uncomfortably small at inline size.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are sound; the issues are implementation-level (panels scaled too small in the canvas, undersized labels/captions, curve and rectangle-top details), so the generator should refine layout, sizing, and geometry.

discrepancies: Layout/whitespace: the three panels are squeezed into a narrow band in the upper-left of the canvas with large empty areas above and below, and the legend strip floats far beneath them — the source is a tight, wide three-panel strip filling the frame.

Panel (b) uses 5 rectangles by default whereas the source shows 6; more noticeably, with the default left-endpoint rule several rectangle tops in the generated (b) overshoot the curve, while the source's (b) shows a mixed inscribed/circumscribed staircase with a taller first-peak block — the staircase silhouette reads differently.

Extra legend ('exact region / rectangles / area missed') and the orange 'area missed' tint are additions not present in the source; the orange tint over overshoot regions is also semantically mislabeled (overshoot is area added, not missed).
The a/b/x/y italic labels and the (a)/(b)/(c) captions are rendered noticeably smaller relative to panel size than in the source, where they are prominent serif italics.
Vertical proportions are slightly compressed: the source curve's hump/trough occupies a taller fraction of the panel height than in the generated panels.
